Stardew Valley, an indie farming simulation game, has captured the hearts of gamers worldwide, establishing itself as a beloved classic in the gaming community. This virtual oasis not only offers a tranquil escape from reality but also provides a myriad of engaging activities that cater to diverse player interests. From tending to crops, raising animals, mining in the depths of the earth, fishing in idyllic waters, to forming meaningful relationships with townsfolk, the game offers a rich tapestry of experiences. Its pixel art style, enchanting soundtrack, and charming characters add to the game's allure, creating a cozy and immersive world that players can easily get lost in. Stardew Valley's open-ended gameplay allows for personalization and creativity, granting players the freedom to shape their virtual farm according to their preferences. The game's attention to detail, depth of content, and the sense of accomplishment derived from building and expanding one's farm make it a truly captivating and rewarding experience. Its seamless integration of farming, crafting, exploration, and social interactions ensures that players are constantly engaged and have a wide array of activities to delve into. The game's emphasis on relaxation and self-paced gameplay provides a soothing and therapeutic experience, allowing players to unwind and escape the stresses of everyday life. Furthermore, Stardew Valley's community-focused approach, where players are encouraged to contribute to the well-being of the town and help their neighbors, fosters a sense of camaraderie and belonging. The game's continuous updates and developer support demonstrate a commitment to its player base, ensuring that there is always something new and exciting to discover in the world of Stardew Valley. With its timeless appeal, infinite replay value, and genuine passion poured into every aspect of its design, Stardew Valley stands as a testament to the sheer brilliance and artistry of indie game development, solidifying its place as one of the best games to ever exist.

A very close and dear friend gifted this game to me and I have been obsessed ever since. The pixel art is beautiful, the seasons are stunning, and the lore is incredible. I was going through a rough time in my life when I first started playing this game and it always made me feel better, even if I could only play for a few minutes. The attention to every little detail is what amazes me about this game. I thought at first getting to know the villagers was just an annoying task, however, I couldn't have been more wrong. Getting to know the villagers and each of their unique personalities, likes, and dislikes keeps the game entertaining and feeling fresh. The villagers aren't portrayed as perfect pixel people, but rather struggles that many people face on a daily basis (addiction/grief/financial struggles/aging). Each season is uniquely beautiful and has a wonderful event (Dance of the Moonlight Jellies is my personal favorite). The game is so inherently relaxing to me, that I listen to the soundtrack when I'm feeling a great deal of stress. My original game was on the switch until I was gifted it on steam. So, it's gonna take me a while because my previous game was my legacy save. I would recommend this game to anyone and give it a 10/10. Eric Barone, the creator, deserves all the appraise he receives.

It's not just a farming game, it has so much story and unique characters, stories, and you can play it however you like! Whether you want to focus on fishing, maybe mining, or Farming! I love the style and art of the game as well, it has just such an enjoyable look to it and the music is easy to listen to and also quite enjoyable. Yes this game may not be for everyone, but for those that like something that's just inbetween story and exploration, this one is just for you. You'll start off limited but you'll find new islands, places, and more! Yes eventually you'll learn everything about the game eventually, but walking away for just a couple months makes playing it again such an amazing experience. Through no fault of your own you awaken the corpse of GLaDoS, the artificial intelligence hell-bent on making life as miserable and scientifically valuable as possible. The reanimated skeleton of Portal’s villain returns 80% corrupted, but still mostly the same. She sneers at you, berates you, calls you fat, ugly, adopted and dumb. She does what she always does: tests you. Everything new to you that is discovered in Portal 2 is inherently old and abandoned: Cave Johnson, the dead CEO of Aperture Science, clings on through whirring tapes, GlaDoS is alive but without a true purpose, and Wheatley is battling demons no-one can validate. Everything within the facility is moving towards a result that is irrelevant because the people to whom it mattered are no longer alive. Aperture Science is a maimed titan clinging on, and your role is to escape it. You are abandoned and forgotten like the machinery you interact with, and there is beyond a shroud of doubt the creeping feeling that you are alone in this. The dread that comes from being within what is ultimately a dying entity is haunting. Furthermore, the sarcastic, dry humour of Portal distances you even further from your surroundings. Not only are you not wanted here, but you are hated for it. Stylistically and narratively Portal 2 is hands down one of the best games ever made. It knows exactly what it is and excels at it.

The world building is also insanely good with countless stunning set pieces, and it really is crazy to think that this game is 14 years old. The soundtrack of the game also builds crazy suspense and the fact that the music changes depending on the environment really makes it feel like the music fits right into the universe. Overall, portal 2 is an amazing game with near perfect storytelling, game play, visuals, characters, and music to create one of the most mind blowing experiences you will ever get to enjoy.

Beautiful sequel! It does not try to amp up the themes that were already masterfully developed in Portal. Instead it provides a flourishing variety of graphical styles and new gameplay that play homage to the first installment while providing a lot of fun and entertainment to the player. While the first game is dark and builds upon the oppressive feeling of loneliness and uncertainty, here you have talkative companions and you feel part of a story with a finale that is more and more anticipated. There is a fantastic comic relief in Wheatley and some psychological introspection about human nature with Glados/Caroline. Moreover the development of the character of Cave Johnson through the recordings and the framed portraits is subtle and remarkable. And the evolution of graphics and technology through the decades as you explore the old labs is really aesthetically pleasing. So in conclusion, really, really recommended game, brilliant and entertaining - just not as iconic, focused, and touching as the first one, which is a masterpiece.

I was NOT expecting to love this game as much as I did. I'm a person who gets seriously stressed out when confronted with something I can't figure out, so puzzle games are usually a pass for me. However, this game had intuitive puzzle design that at times felt overwhelming, but when picked apart was really quite simple for the most part. I will say however that the test chambers were quite repetitive, and the segments outside of chambers were the parts that I enjoyed the most. It also felt like the game dragged on a little bit, but 4-5 hours really isn't terrible. I loved the character design and how each one was somewhat lovable/understandable in their own way (even though there were only 3 characters if you count the defects as 1 character). I feel like the game was somewhat lacking in protagonist character design, though, because it really just felt like our character was a vessel for the story to progress, when we should have been an interlocking part. I guess the game leaves it up to the player to be the protagonist's personality? Anyway, final sequence was clever and also somewhat heartwarming. I just love when games go and make their own lyrical soundtracks, it makes everything so much more cinematic (just take a look at Mirror's Edge!). Anyway, all in all pretty fun game and a story that actually wasn't too bad. (Also, the part where he kills you did get a pretty good laugh out of me :))

Gotta say, that was an odd experience. For such a beloved and oft-lauded title, I found this to be a notch below the first game on the whole. The first act was solid, on even footing with Portal 1's puzzles and had an interesting story (+funny new cast member in the form of Wheatley). Then the second act hit, and I was thoroughly disappointed in both the quality of the puzzles and the environmental design. Browns and grays all around made my time spent in the "dungeon" of Aperture Science largely miserable, and some obtuse puzzle gatekeeping made that even worse. The saving grace was Cave Johnson's funny bits, but even that got a little much after a while. Then the third act blew me away with how awesome it was, even a step above the best of the first game. So yeah, a weird ride for sure. I've landed on an 8/10 for this one: 9/10 first act, 5/10 second act, and 10/10 third act comes out to be about that. Very little desire to replay this one, though co-op is pretty enticing.

Portal 2 is a great sequel to a great game and I would consider it as good, if not better than the original, as of course should be expected. Portal 2 continues on with same hilarious writing, supported by amazing voice acting. The gameplay also is up to par with original (meaning great), while also adding new mechanics to the puzzles. Visually it is an improvement from the original and depending on the chapter the appropriate atmosphere is there, helped by both visuals and sound design. The only negative, which is probably a nitpick, is that if memory serves me right, the first Portal's loading screens were much more seamless, though that probably is just a result of the upgrade in visuals... plus the loading times weren't long, so as I said, probably just a nitpick. As for co-op, I personally didn't try it out, so I can't speak on it. A last note, I do recommend to anyone curious about Portal 2 to first try out the first Portal. Other than that in my opinion Portal is still a great game, as you can see in this review, I compared Portal 2 a lot to the first Portal, that and Portal 2 is direct sequel, meaning that the writing of Portal 2 will hit harder if you played or at the very least watched or know about the story of the first. In conclusion, I enjoyed my time with Portal 2 and I recommend it!

There are a some grievances: the game is still a linear Point A to Point B simulator with very little deviation, the humour is very hit-or-miss, and about 1/3 of the campaign is spent pixel-hunting for a tiny, white surface far into the background that you can shoot a portal onto. Still a good experience over a decade later, although this game is not as peerless as others claim it to be.

You can also create your own levels with an in-game designer, as well as play other people's levels as well, with very popular custom maps and even coded in tools like the gravity-gun from Half-Life. Play through every level again but with a twist... be timed, be forced to use as least portals as possible... and beat people's records online. Play Portal 2, it's great.

If you like simple and snappy gameplay, are looking for something new to pick up for your steamdeck, or wish poker was more interesting thanks to magical jokers, then this is the game for you. The only thing I wish it had was a stronger sense of permanent progression. Outside of gathering a stronger sense of understanding and overall strategy, your fiftieth run feels pretty similar to your first run. The different decks can offer some interesting twists, but I'm still missing the sense of gradual progression and accumulation of abilities that are present in my favorite rogue-likes. Even with that, I still highly recommend picking this up.

Logic dictates that if you get another joker that has a similar description but without the "... when scored" that you would think that you get the bonus for every card that fits the description even if it is a card that does not score but this is not the case like with the Flower Pot joker. In the end this means that you have to check up in the Internet for every card you do not know by heart how it works to make sure it works like one would think.

I like to call this a deck builder for people who don't normally play deck builders. That's what it is for me at least. It takes the three things that have normally kept me away from deck builders - the need to maximize a build permanently, the learning curve, and competition - and eliminated them. I really enjoy "push your luck" games along with games where you are aiming to beat your personal best, so this really has done the trick for me. Additionally, I appreciate that the learning curve is lessened by being based off of traditional poker hands but it's really not a poker game at all. This game is not only fun to play but an interesting masterclass in game design. If you've ever been curious about deck builders by have been weary of the factors I mentioned above, I'd definitely recommend Balatro.

The game is amazing, music, combat, a very distinctive and beautiful artsyle. It takes an interesting approach to the genre, instead of a million unique items gotten at random, you pick one of 6 main weapons and will get upgrades to you character and weapon, thus it is more skill based and open to making actual builds without being insanely random. The gameplay is great, that's almost a given, if you like rougue-likes it is a no brainer, but what is most interesting to me is it's dialogue and narrative. I've never seen a rogue-like try this hard to tell a narrative, using the genre to its advantage, it is one of the best things about the game, the sheer amount of voice acted dialouge here is immpressive, all written and acted extremely well. It's one of the only rogue-likes where aside from doing runs for the sake of gameplay, I am invested in these character and how the story will play out. That is what makes the game special, there is so much depth to everything here, this world feels alive and rich and full of character. I could talk about it for a while but needless to say, it is one of the cornerstones of the genre, up there with the best of them, Worth every penny.

Hades is a Rougelite in the clothing of greek mythology and my first game of this genre, the characteristic of the game which is to fail and "lose" progress was not so appealing to me. However, the nice music, story telling, charming art style and an entertaining combat system with an avoiding "dash" was astonishing fun to play. If you pair this with some skill and a healthy hunger to collect achievements you´re ready to go. Let´s dive a bit deeper into Hades without too much spoil. The characters were excellently brought to life through voice acting, this was a nice surprise for me, making the game world feel more immersive. When you interact with those characters, in some cases you can choose... yes you can! (your actions have consequences). The arsenal you wield can be enhanced alongside some bonuses which make your runs smoother, oh and not to forget the interesting interior decorations of the underworld. If you do not skip through all dialogues but immerse yourself in the story, you maybe surprised how many emotions will be woken... and even carried into the real life. The weak point of the game in my opinion is that it seems something is missing or could be more elaborated. Maybe there will be a link to Hades 2 where the story connects? For long time motivation it would be nice to have a larger choise then only getting the last overpriced piece of the underworld collection. This is not my cup of tea... is this genre made for long time motivation? perhaps you simply move on to the next Roguelite game or wait for the sequel? All in all I had a lot of fun with Hades. From time to time it can be quite a challenge, in such situations it is important not to lose the joy of playing the game, trying out a new style of play, or taking a break to strategize can be helpful to overcome the struggle. It´s nice to see some developers make solid effort in their work, trying to create a masterpiece. If you appreciate the Roguelite genre and you are willing to give Hades a try you won´t be disappointed. Have fun and enjoy Hades!

Hades was probably my first real rogue-like game that I had ever played. I played it on my Nintendo Switch at first only to get the first ending. I decided to get it on PC to try and push for the 10 times completion for the true ending. I definitely enjoyed that process a lot, and trying out combinations, and then building the relationships with the different NPCs of the game. This is especially great when characters remark at your repeated deaths early on, and their reactions especially after beating through it. There's probably so much more that I still haven't really been able to see in the game, but I believe I got a good amount out of it, and I definitely recommend for anyone to try it out. It definitely gave me a good introduction into the rogue-like genre though, and it's a whole lot of fun once you understand how things work in the game. You might want to do a bit of your own research like I did after running through your own builds, or otherwise just in completely blind and I'm sure you'll still be able to enjoy it that way. I also really enjoy Greek mythology, and if that's something you dig, you'll dig this game too.

As I reach the end of my natural life cycle with Hades, I only have good things reserved to say about this game. As of writing this I have 100% completed the game, and enjoyed it every step of the way. I don't have dozens of rogue-likes played, but I'm familiar to the genre. Hades' take on rogue-likes has truly paved the way for a multitude of other game formulas. There is never a run through Hades that will be like the last, this is the game's most celebrated mechanic. It keeps things fresh while simultaneously forcing the player to learn the different dynamics of its gameplay, albeit in a fun way. It's a game that isn't afraid to humble the player regularly, and also let them be insanely overpowered. If you're the type of person that loves addictive gameplay loops, crunching numbers, unique character designs, a fun story and seemless-smooth gameplay... then Hades is absolutely worth the purchase.

The story is sort of like DDLC which I also enjoyed playing, but this one is a lot more interactive, and geometric... obviously. The game has a bunch of hidden things around the whole game, collectables, games, , which adds a good amount of replayability, it took me about another 4 hours to 100% but that was with a guide, I'm sure that it would take a bit longer if you tried to find everything yourself. This is a seriously good horror game with compelling story, characters, level design, and gameplay. It keeps getting fresh, with new mini games as well as new ways of getting scary. I personally can't stand horror games that make you constantly hide from something, and this game has one such section that is actually well executed and then it moves on. Sections where you must run away from a chaser through narrow corridors? Yes, it does that well too, but then it moves on to the next. PT references with looping corridors? It does that well too but then moves on to something else. It also has interesting commentary on the nature of games and life and routine, discussing the idea of "being trapped". Certainly a unique experience worth playing. It's fairly priced and has hours of replayability (many endings and choices) with collectibles that help build up the world of the game.

Dumbfounded on how this game has received all the praise it has. A word I see being repeated a lot is "polished". Here, I would agree. The game has solid art direction; there's plenty of charm to the 3D anime style, and the soundtrack's quite beautiful, honestly. But, like many other polished things, it's all soft around the edges. The actual substance of this game is nothing but a collection of already done-to-death horror game mechanics... and it's not a stew either, like a lovely dish with all these mechanics served together. No, it's more like... a buffet of raw ingredients? All are given their own sections; there's a P.T section, there's a Weeping Angels section, there's a The Witness section, weirdly enough... not even the non-horror elements can stop themselves from being horribly derivative. Worst of all is how short they are; you don't even get time to have fun with the stuff they stole! There's a shooter section that'll make you laugh your ass off with how ridiculously lackluster it is; at times it almost feels like the devs are in on the joke.

Miside, what a game this was.. I honestly, genuinely can't find the words to describe this game, it was just.. flawless, amazing, fantastic... there's so much i can say about this game, i could rant about it for days. There's so much you can do in this game, looking around and interacting with the environment, choose your own text, and much more. You're a random guy who has a miserable life, eat, work, sleep repeat. One day, you get a message of a game called Miside, you download it and encounter Mita for the first time, she's a friendly, beautiful character you take care of. You help her with necessities and moving things, as time goes on you grow more addicted to the game. Eventually, Mita wants to meet in person, remember, this is a character inside a game. One day, she asks you to look up, there you are, inside of the game. You're in an outdated version of the game unfortunately, so you can't see Mita, yet.. You haft to find items to put on a teleporting device that'll allow you to get to the latest version of the game, once you reach v1.9, you finally meet Mita. The woman you took care of inside the game for over a month, right there infront of you. She's overjoyed to meet you, while you're left confused and scared of what's going on. Mita will follow you around the house as you explore, she'll cook you a meal along with the help of yours. She gives you a sauce called " Love Sauce " which you took it as a joke, after eating your meal everything starts to static and get glitchy, Mita will give you pills to help with the sudden effects. You're having a good time with Mita, however you're still scared about how everything happened so suddenly. Who knows how long you've been inside the game, you finally sit down and play a console game with her and some cards. This is where everything changes.. You start hearing banging inside the wardrobe, you ignore the sounds at first, but eventually they get loud enough you haft to say something about it. Mita says she doesn't hear anything, her face frowns after you mention the wardrobe, you go to check the sound but she stops you before entering, making excuses of why you can't look in there. Eventually she'll give you an option to look inside, if you accept looking in, well, you just made a fatal mistake.. and a big discovery...

I highly recommend this game. Although not very long, it is beautifully done, with interesting story, several likable characters with different personalities, well done scenes and packed with details and easter eggs. There are few jumpscares, but they aren't just appearing instantly out of nowhere in front of your face (even though it is quite close to that maybe once) and aren't accompanied by a disgusting, eardrum-tearing sound. Some people might be disappointed by low difficulty, and dangerous encounters with antagonists might be longer, but I can mostly overlook it because of how the feel of the game constantly changes as you progress and it doesn't feel monotonous (well, with exception of those parts where it was intentional). It is amazing what the two developers have done. Since they had to cut some content because of not having enough time, I'm really looking forward when more content will be added (hoping also for more endings). I certainly do not regret buying this nice game at full price.

The story was well made, the gameplay was generally enjoyable and surprisingly varied. Almost every area had some unique mechanic or minigame in it, which is hard to pull off well, but this game does it. Each segment gets its time in the spotlight but does not overstay its welcome. The areas also looked visually great and varied. I personally really liked the areas that appeared more open. The game had a good mix of horror and chill segments, which are spread out in a good way so that the non-horror segments amplify the horror segments and vice-versa. Very polished as well, I encountered no bugs or lag. Overall, would recommend, and absolutely lives up to the hype. 9/10

This game... is probably my second favorite game that you could spend a ridiculous amount of time on and not regret it. It's got a surplus of things do to and things you will never get to do with one game, so basically, you can repeat it many times and always have a different experience. I at one point had a dude that sucked at everything but research and animals that tamed a fox, and a wolf attempted to kill said fox, but failed. Then it tried again and one-shot the poor fox. I considered killing the wolf, but for some reason decided to tame it, and with a ONE PERCENT CHANCE of success, the guy tamed the wolf and the wolf later became a very valuable asset, even taking a fatal bullet to the head during the last few hours of my colony's time on the planet to protect the one building the ship to escape. So yeah, the game goes VERY deep into the smallest decisions. I don't like how it can sometimes be tricky to stay on top of the colonists mood, because there are some events that you can't control, like an affair. There is nothing you can do there (besides exile the cheater), so in that way it mimics reality, which I do like. A very thought out game with lots of AI usage and it has a sense of survival to it as well, forcing you to sacrifice luxury over more important things. Also, they have a cool saving system where you can save your game before big events, like a battle, to head back if you made a mistake, or to see what would happen if you did something different, and if you don't like this, you could simply turn it off with the push of a button! Which reminds me, the experience you have playing can be completely changed by what settings you have on, so I highly recommend looking at a tutorial before playing, trust me, its worth it. To finalize, I would recommend this game to anyone who likes strategy games and has some extra time on there hands, because this game can take a while, and also, don't get any mods without thoroughly looking at them. And quick warning, this game has some lovey stuff in it, not visually or anything, but it's there. I hope you find this review helpful and have a great day!

While many games find their ultimate fulfillment upon their completion, RimWorld shines brilliantly with purpose throughout the journey itself. In the 1,000 hours I've played, I only ever "beat" the game twice out of hundreds of runs. It's not that it's even that difficult of a game (though you can certainly set it up in such a way), but that each run is its own story, and some of those stories don't find their end in the credits roll; victory is not the condition for enjoyment. From tragedies to comebacks, slice-of-life to epic odyssey, dramatic thriller to slapstick comedy, there's always more to tell, always more to see. RimWorld grants the wish of an avid reader having reached the end of a great book: A new page at every turn.

Even when you start a run with a specific idea in mind, the game could end up going in a totally different direction than you planned, but in the best way possible. I am generally a cozy gamer that plays life sims and farming sims, but this game could easily appeal to survival horror or just survival game fans in general. I do not mean easy as in not difficult, as the difficulty is definitely brutal at times - I mean easy as in less time spent in tedious setup tasks. The replayability is very high as well. The genre is an excellent mix of high-tech sci fi with low-level survivalism, which too few games really get right, but this nails it. The stories that come out of this game are endless and memorable. I must say I actually don't like the additions to the game, I prefer the original content and balance. This is probably my favorite game of the last decade. Building a colony from scratch on an alien world, trying to face down hardship after hardship is a really good formula. The updates made to the game over time have been mostly welcome. The modding community is large and active. You can mod the game to experience almost any colony fantasy that you can imagine: build a shogunate village in medieval times, form a space marine chapter from 40K, mine into mountainsides with your dwarf fortress ripoff - whatever you want to experience, it's possible. The game has a lot of different systems that work well together, and the modding community has even added more systems that can be integrated into the game like vehicles and combat overhaul mechanics. Would recommend to someone who enjoys dwarf fortress or other colony sim games, but even if you are more of a general strategy fan, you might enjoy this game.

I liked this game quite a bit. My opinion of it evolved over my 66 hours of playtime. At first it was interesting, but then I felt like the combat was a bit clunky and not so fun, but once I allowed myself to start to upgrade my character (duh) it unlocked the gameplay dramatically. I wouldn't say it was an amazing unmissable game, but the story was engaging and the voice acting was pretty good (English) and the gameplay became fairly enjoyable for me once I allowed myself to power up. I did have to use a mod to adjust mouse movement controls (NAIOM) because it was apparently not a great console port - although I ended up using a controller eventually for most of the hacking as it was just better for that part. I also used the "Special K" mod from the start which is apparently highly recommended. I also updated the cutsecenes to 1440p (nexus mods) as the native ones are pretty rough looking compared to the gameplay graphics at 1440p at least. For achievement hunters, there are really no technically missable achievements as everything that is not story based can be "bought" with in game money after the 3rd route of the game, though as I played through this game I realized it deserved better than that from me, so I did it all the official way.
The storyline is super engaging. It's challenging enough to keep me interested, but not so hard that it's frustrating. I highly recommend checking it out!

The story, world and characters are fairly interesting, but the gameplay just isn't good enough for it to be worth it in my opinion. The combat gets very repetitive quickly, and they make some weird choices that just ruin it for me. Healing items don't replenish after death, and are extremely cheap, so if you're struggling to fight a boss or something, you can just go fish for 10-20 minutes and buy a billion repair kits to spam during the fight. Also, many of the bosses are just really boring to fight, and one of them had an unskippable cutscene and a like 2-minute run before you could retry. Additionally, death is very punishing, you have these chips that you use to improve damage and health and stuff, which is a pretty cool system, but when you die all equipped chips drop and if you die again before picking them up, you lose them. These will usually be what you've been grinding for all game, and if you lose them, you obviously won't be able to beat whoever killed you anymore. On top of that, when picking back up your body, you first press a button, then the game pauses to ask what you want to do with the body, then a fairly long animation plays while you can take damage, then it asks you if you want to re-equip all the stuff, which you obviously do, and now you're finally back in the action, which is just really annoying. There are some more weird decision like this, but I won't get into all of them. I'm about 60% through the story, and I'll just be watching like a NieR:Automata all cutscenes full movie youtube video or something to see the rest of it because the gameplay is just not worth it.

Nier: Automata is one of those games where it is an underrated masterpiece, despite having sold 8 million copies in Februrary 2024. It's the staple of the series of never-ending albino human-like non-humans fighting some threat, garnished with a hint of existentialism and philosophy.

Nier: Automata does a lot and only seems to suffers for it in a handful of very small ways, the most glaring of which are its many invisible walls. Though you can double jump and mantle your way across the obstacle-riddled environments, there’s little distinction between climbable surfaces and unclimbable barriers even in areas that look like they’re absolutely built to be scaled. Its maps are filled with secretive nooks and crannies which makes the inevitable backtracking more tolerable, but actually accessing those spaces can be deeply frustrating, and the cumbersome 3D world map doesn’t offer much help in that regard. After two dozen hours I still struggled to know where I could and couldn’t go, and finding the correct path up or down occasionally involved the equivalent of beating my head against a wall until one of the two finally gave.

Keep in mind, you die in around two-three hits on hard mode. And a boss then shows that up that is a giant claw with two attacks and it covers the whole arena. You are barely taught the controls; I had no clue how to avoid one of its attacks. I struggled to dodge their arena covering attacks and died and got sent right back to the bullet hell section. I probably spent about 30 mins on that singular run only to get sent back to the beginning. Funny enough, when you press pause, you see a quick save button but you can't press it! This game has some of the most ludicrous game design I have ever seen. I can't wait to get my money back.

As someone who loves the entire world of the franchise you need to start with Nier Replicant to "fully" appreciate both games. I have 100% both games on xbox and about to do both on steam. NieR Replicant's story is one of the best ever written and has one of the best end games of all time. The last hour and a half to two hours is an emotional payout of everything you've done and people you've met with countless boss fights, betrayal, and two plot twists. I was there day 1 of NieR Automata's release after playing the original NieR. While Automata is in a different weight class with it's story, I still felt it falls short compared to the original; especially with the plot twists having less of an effect on the player; except maybe 1 of them near the end. It's a great game for what it is, but hopping in with Automata is just the lesser of two great stories as well as taking place after NieR giving some major things away. There are 3 characters in Automata that make reappearances and just by seeing them you spoil the fates of those characters and spoil 1 of the plot twists from Nier Replicant. The only thing I'd truly give to Automata doing better would be combat, even with my own personal bias to Replicant's combat, the community agrees that Automata's is better. PLAY BOTH if you're getting into the franchise but please start NieR Replicant first. I would say start with Drakengard but the games are old and haven't gotten a remake yet. (Drakengard 3 leads to Drakengard 1. Drakengard 1 leads to Drakengard 2 or NieR Replicant based on which ending. NieR Replicant leads to NieR Automata.)

It is not a great slasher, and bullet-hell mechanics are really burdensome, it does not have the most genius, logical or well-polished story, and, at the very end, the scenario definitely runs out of steam. The graphics are fine for its age, and the game (at least now) is bug-free and mechanically plays very nicely. Seemingly "B" grade, but the way everything is put together and mixed up, plus amazing themed music, make it a superb piece for those who are looking for emotional and entertaining game.

The game’s standout strength is its narrative, which explores existential questions about consciousness, free will, and the nature of existence, often leaving players with a sense of introspection. The gameplay is exhilarating, featuring fluid, combo-heavy combat with a mix of genres, from action to top-down shooter and even bullet-hell segments. The world design is beautifully bleak, with a haunting atmosphere that perfectly complements the game’s story, while the soundtrack, composed by Keiichi Okabe, elevates every emotional moment. However, the game is not without its drawbacks—its repetitive structure, especially across multiple playthroughs, can feel tiresome for some, as the core gameplay loop doesn’t vary enough between routes. The pacing is sometimes uneven, and while the story is compelling, certain characters lack deeper development. Additionally, technical issues, particularly on PC, can detract from the overall experience. Despite these flaws, Nier: Automata is a unique and thought-provoking title, one that’s likely to stay with you long after you’ve finished it, thanks to its philosophical depth and unforgettable emotional moments.

This game is an absolute masterpiece, on the surface it looks like any other JRPG that can be dismissed as Yoko Taro telling all of us the type of women he's into (Which I'll be honest might have some truth to it.). But this game is a rabbit hole, right when you think the game ends, it just gets deeper, each time your jaw drops with what is really going on. This game loves to keep you on your toes, changing over and over again, the last 30 minutes of gameplay is different from the next 30 minutes (In main quest) I really really admire this game for breaking industry norms, not only does the designers break it, but they mold it, and break it again. They test the limits of their given genre, which is what game developers should be doing. Everything in this game is carefully put together, the story, the music, the relationships, everything. This is modern day art piece, and you are the viewer. With the end, this game does not fail to make me stare point blank thinking what the hell I just played as the credits roll. The music in this game is outrageously good for no reason, there's a few points in the game where I just think to myself "Did they make this scene around the music or the music around the game??" I am actually shocked they don't sell the album on steam. There are some cringe JRPG elements in this game at some points, However the good outweighs the bad a thousand fold. I cannot recommend this game enough. What we have here is a gem of a game, and you should play it. TaTa and Fair well.

Story however is where this game excels and well it's amazing, I promise this game isn't just the hot lady you've seen on the hub, actually give it a shot, themes of philosophy and purpose are abundant and it will definitely leave you questioning the important things. good/very

Really glad I finally got around to completing Nier Automata. This game is incredible from both a gameplay and story direction perspective. The dynamic camera and alternating combat styles kept the game fresh even when fighting and traversal got tedious at times. Although I was apprehensive about having to do 3 playthroughs to unlock the true ending, the payoff was immensely satisfying even as someone who already knew significant story spoilers. Each route should be faster than the last. One caveat that I need to mention is that skipping repeated combat sections or not doing side quests will leave you severely underleveled for the subsequent routes. So unlike me, take your time and help these NPCs out as Himmel the Hero would. That aside, it would be a cardinal sin to not mention the music in this game. As someone who treats most music like beeps and boops, Nier has a truly special OST that is not only memorable but incredibly immersive. If you are on the fence because you have already been spoiled, gave up in the first two routes, or only know of Nier via 2B's butt, all I can say is trust in Yoko Taro to deliver you a masterpiece.

Is this game perfect? Not by a long shot but I find myself talking about this game in my discord with my friends like it has spiritually shook me. More specifically, I find myself marveling at the enemy AI protocol. Simply put, the enemy AI design is an astonishing accomplishment. This game possesses quite possibly the absolute best demonstration of enemy AI I have ever encountered in my brief existence on this planet. I cannot commend the developer enough about the subtle nuances of the AI and its ability to adapt to you or the player population. Of course it has all the given attributes of modern AI, it is omniscient, it has ESP, it undoubtedly reads inputs, it can compute complex data quick enough to change the move set employed or the targeting priority BUT it is executed in such a refined and subdued manner. It makes for a great teacher, which I would think would be the ideal enemy AI concept. You will fail a good bit HOWEVER it never felt unbeatable. For me, it never once felt insurmountable. NOT ONCE. The only thing I felt was the unyielding motivation to log in day after day in my endeavor to master the combat system and beat that wretched AI. The AI in this game, is beautiful. Something truly remarkable has happened here and I cannot recommend this game enough if you like a challenging game, with an incredibly rewarding and satisfying combat system.

It's a pretty game but poorly designed. I would go as far as saying incompetently designed. You're a Space Marine with tissue-paper armour who can be killed by a swarm of Hormagaunts. And this will happen frequently due to poor controls and horrible game play systems. You’ll die, but not because of a lack of skill or a failure to ‘git good; you’ll get killed because your marine cannot do anything when surrounded. When he swings, he steps forward, deeper into the swarm. You cannot control your movement leading to frustrating tactical compromises. You can AOE, but it requires at least one swing first, so the melee mechanics are designed to get you killed. There is little to no control over your character. You just get pummelled over and over again, especially if you’re like me and play on the harder difficulties. The whole power fantasy thing is gone. You feel more powerful being a guardsman in Dark Tide than you do playing a Space Marine in this game. It would be okay if there was a game mechanic that could be mastered to get you out of such situations, but there isn’t. All you can do is reload the game and use your new magical foresight to know a horde is coming, and try to thin it out at range. Even that is horribly implemented. You can’t just switch weapons. You have a button for melee, another button for range and another button for aiming. So, you can’t just switch to a Bolter and press Mouse1 to fire and then switch to a chainsword and press Mouse1 to swing because that would make too much sense in this horrible game. No, you have to bind each function to a different key, as though context was a concept far too complicated for the devs. This makes for many awkward combat encounters where you aim your Bolter and then, rather than firing the weapon, you instead accidentally swing your sword. Even the finishers are repetitive and lacklustre, becoming events that, you guessed it, take away your control so you can be surrounded and finished-off by Hormagaunts. It is also a horribly linear game with an absolutely brain-dead story. The linearity is particularly off-putting because your character makes really dumb decisions all the time, as do the other characters. I have absolutely no idea how this game is popular. Seriously, it’s a linear grind with horribly designed combat and a story which makes me feel like I've lost braincells. I’d urinate on this game if I didn’t think that would be an insult to the comparative dignity of uric acid.

The story wants to be good, but the AI leaves a lot to be desired. The main campaign is rather short with only 5 or 6 missions total, with the rest of the story being filled in with about 9 "Ops" missions that take place simultaneously with the main story. The main campaign allows you to try out various weapons and gear as the story directs which in turn allows you to make semi-informed decisions about how you want to equip each class of avatar for the Ops. Problem is, someone didn't seam to understand how to describe the difficulty settings, and as a result "Minimal" (easy mode) feels like Halo 3's "Heroic" difficulty from 2007. Unless you find a Guardian Relic, you can only go down twice before you fail the mission. Playing with friends must be the main way to play, but if friends aren't available you can either go online with randos or play solo and have the AI fill in the other two spots of the party. Even on Minimal difficulty, being swarmed is extremely easy, which leads to excessive stunlocking that will quickly consume your two "lives", and the AI "allies" apparently focus more on their own survival rather than taking out the various enemies, forcing you to do every bit of heavy lifting. The campaign story is a noticeable improvement on SM1, if perhaps still fairly simplistic; it reuses the same exact artifact from the first game as its McGuffin. It pits you against a Tyranid hive fleet and the Thousand Sons traitor legion as well as the arrogance and obstinance of the Adeptus Mechancus across three planets (a jungle world, a hive world and a burial world). The PvE missions are partly woven into the narrative as the adventures of squads Lieutenant Titus dispatches to attack additional objectives his own half-squad can't cover - at one point in the plot, a Campaign mission is simultaneous with Operations; there are only a few missions, however, and the devs are slowly adding more as free updates. The campaign is serviceable, with later missions playing off strongly on pathos and fanservice and macho chest-beating... which is what you sign up for in an Astartes-centered 40k game, wasn't it? A significant addition is a character arc centered around a simple narrative of trust vs caginess in a pressing situation, creating drama within Titus's squad stemming from his own unwillingness to share about his past - it's about as much as you can do with the single-minded superhuman warriors anyway, but it builds off the plot of SM1, it's a lot, lot more than there was in that game... and it's bloody satisfying.

Ignore all comparisons to Helldivers 2(another great game); this game is nothing like it and has its own amazing and unique charm. The combat is so satisfying. Only issue would be replayability, but tbh that is not an issue until you hit like 30-40 hours. Each level is hand crafted which is why it may get repetative playing it over and over again, but there are a lot of levels with different difficulties(meaning different boss fights) and so many different classes to level up. Also, there is a PvP as I mentioned, which I think needs improvement but is on a good track. The devs also released a lot of plans and roadmaps which looks promising. Overall, maybe you won't be playing this game continuously for like months on end, but definitely for weeks on end every now and then. And you know what? That's okay! Some games are not huge time sinks but masterpieces at the same time; this game is a great example. GOTY contender imho. 8.5/10(-1.5 purely for the PvP).

On the gameplay front, Space Marine 2 strikes a near-perfect balance between fast-paced action and strategic combat. The game flawlessly blends visceral melee combat with satisfying ranged gunplay, allowing players to chain together devastating combos with ease, while still maintaining a sense of weight and power fitting for a Space Marine. The improved enemy AI and variety of Tyranid foes add layers of complexity, requiring thoughtful engagement rather than mere button-mashing. Visually, Space Marine 2 is a tour de force. The environments are gorgeously detailed, from the desolate battlefields to the grotesque alien hives, all rendered with stunning fidelity. The Unreal Engine 5 brings not only the large-scale battles to life but also captures the grim, oppressive atmosphere that defines the Warhammer 40,000 universe. Add to this an intense score and immersive sound design, and you have a game that doesn’t just succeed as a sequel but firmly cements itself as a standout title in both the Warhammer franchise and the wider action game genre.

It's a solid package that is only being added too, with the 7th operation mission already added with more on the way, along with new weapons and multiplayer match types. The Long Version: I miss when every game release was like this, you get a full single player campaign that took me about 11 hours to complete and that you can play entirely in co-op with up to 2 friends! You get a full left 4 dead style set of mini-campaigns for co-op with cosmetic and skill tree based customisation for classes unique to the mode. Finally, you also get a full PvP mode too! Sure this mode is clearly underbaked and not well balanced, but it's still fun! and it's not trying to be anything else, they just knew that we would all want to pit space marines against space marines to they tossed it in for free! The core gameplay loop is simple, but satisfying and fun, the story is pretty messy, but some of the character moments are great, and the visuals are truly stunning! The art direction is just fantastic, this is the first 40k game I've played to truly capture the grand, epic scale that makes it so appealing, while darktide captured the aesthetic and tone perfecctly, it stuck to smaller scale environments with a more limited scope. Space Marine 2 blows it out of the water, giving you battlefields stretching to the horizon, literal HUNDREDS of enemies at once really selling the super human power fantasy of cleaving through hordes of weaker enemies at once and the insane scale of the world, with buildings and ships covering the entire sky and all of this with enough engine optimisation that I was able to run the entire game on a mid range system at a steady 60fps with all settings on high! The lowest frame dip I ever saw was only 50fps, which is really incredible when you take into account how good this game looks. The only "microtransaction" is a season's pass that is just cosmetics, and which they have said the profits will go back into the development of the free content they are adding later on! I would love to go back to releasing games like this, it launches with a full suite of content, you pay once up front and get everything you want, and it incentives you to keep playing by having a long list of unlocks that you can ONLY unlock by just playing the game, rather than a never ending stream of limited time paid content that tries to tap into your FOMO to get you to keep playing and spending more money. On top of that it is the best representation of the 40k universe in a game yet! Even with some of it's minor flaws like repetitive gameplay by the end of the story mode or a forgettable plot, it does so much right and shows you so much you've never seen before in a game that it cannot get anything but a full recommendation from me!

I’ll definitely continue playing it alone and with friends but if somebody tells me they don’t want to buy it, I really can’t blame them especially if they’re on midrange hardware that should realistically run this game at 1080p/60fps natively. Wilds probably should have been cancelled and then developed on the REX engine instead with Ichinose’s next game to fill the gap. It’s just too ambitious for what the RE engine is capable of unfortunately. At the very least it should have been delayed for half a year, but Capcom rushed it out the door to appease shareholders. So now it is what it is and I’m not sure if the team will be able to fix all of the huge problems this game has. I really hope they can and they prove me wrong, but that’s not what happened with Dragon’s Dogma 2. If Wilds does reach a state where the good outweighs the bad then I’ll update my review but until then I can’t recommend a $70 game with such high hardware demands that pushes the envelope so little.

Made it to HR 100 recently and I can say that Wilds isn’t quite as big or grand as World but it has some polish and convenience that I wish World had. All cutscenes are skippable which is a big plus for me (I downloaded a mod to skip them in World for my second playthrough). Difficulty feels generally easier than World but it’s pretty easy to seek out high difficulty monsters if you prefer and even some of the harder non tempered monsters are still able to kill me in endgame if I’m not careful. The story doesn’t feel as long as World but you also don’t have to do super long Zorah Magdaros missions or scour the map for footprints over and over again so I don’t think it’s necessarily a bad thing. I’ve been enjoying endgame and the new weapon crafting system. It’s nice to be able to craft a T8 weapon of any type at the end of the game without going through the entire weapon upgrade tree. Part of the difficulty being a bit easier is that monsters are more exploitable with the wound system and other environmental factors but I think it’s fun to feel like you’re using your knowledge to exploit the monster. It reminds me of the posture system in souls games a lot which is a very exploitable system and feels good without making the game feel easy. Wilds is a win because if you do a firework emote the support hunters will do it too and the fishing wudwud will cheer if you catch a big fish near him and that’s all you need really.

I put in about 75 hours and I suspect this is what the average player will put in before the current base game (as of this review, before TU1) grows tiring, plus or minus 10-12 hours depending on experience. Just 1 or 2 truly endgame hunts would have completely changed the game, but the endgame weapon system for min maxing has almost no function currently since tier 8 weapons handle everything just fine and tier 3 gems drop like candy. I do trust that the current sandbox will provide its intended experience, which is to introduce newer players to the world and give them difficult bosses before TU's start to be rolled out. Combat difficulty is more player oriented then game system enforced. Meaning difficulty is mainly on the player to accept. For series veterans I would strongly recommend waiting for a sale while newer players are good to go so long as they can functionally run the game. MH games tend to have the vast majority of their content released as title updates and the master rank dlc that release 1-2 years after the game. This was the case with with MH World and its dlc Iceborne and it was also the case with MH Rise and its dlc Sunbreak. The best time to get into any MH game is 2-3 years after release when all the content is out and you can get the game and its dlc on sale. World and Rise are both often on sale so they may be better investments for the time being but if you're patient then Wilds is definitely worth getting into

This is my first monster hunter game. I didn't really know what to expect going into it. I was pleasantly surprised. The game play is rock solid, crafting and upgrade system addicting, and the animations are very high quality. The story was fine but I honestly did not care and ended up skipping a lot of the cut scenes toward the second half of the story because I just wanted to fight cool monsters. I've heard performance being a major issue for some people. I have a 4080 ti. I havent really had any performance issues as far as fps goes, but i have had several crashes over 40 hrs and a handful of visual bugs. Both were infrequent enough to say they didnt impact MY overall enjoyment of the game but I feel like I have a pretty high tolerance for these types of issues. I have no reference for how hard or complicated some of the previous games are, but the difficulty is fine for me. I enjoy challenging games a lot, which this game is definitely not, but once you get to the end game you have to pay attention and have the right gear to efficiently kill stuff. That being said ive only failed one quest in my entire play time, and i think i would enjoy the game a bit more if it was more challenging. The amount of systems working is a bit overwhelming for a first time player of monster hunter, but if youve been playing video games for awhile or youre a vet of the series youll be fine. Just read stuff and pay attention to what the game is telling you to do. Overall, love this game. Very hooked on the end game loop right now trying to craft high level stuff. 8.5 /10. Excellent game.
performance issues aside, the game has so much QoL compared to previous titles that the combat feels incredibly fun to play.

Absolutely loving the game so far. While the story might be as interesting as Worlds story, it still has been decent. People have been complaining about the difficulty but it hasn't felt any easier than World, but it does feel a little harder than Rise at least. It seems the complaints are coming from players that have played an insane amount in the past games, where I have around 300+ hours in World and 200 in Rise, so I do not find the game to be easy at all and it seems to have a much more leveled difficulty which I think is the best direction the game could go. The game has been running quite well on my 4070, on high and highest settings (This is with DLSS at Quality and Frame Gen on) Getting around 80-120 fps, depending on the area. Frames have been smooth enough that I haven't seen any massive slowdown while fighting anything, which for me is a good thing. My only real complaint so far is a lack of an area where a team could hang out/eat in, and I loved the housing in the previous games, especially Iceborne. Hoping thats something that could come at a later date.

I will begin this review by stating that I have put close to 6000hrs into the MH series (4000ish of which is in MH4U) in the last decade or so. I adore Monster Hunter and the series has long since earned my loyalty, but it has lost any loyalty I have now. This game is simply awful at being a Monster Hunter game. It feels like it attempts to iterate on World, the weakest entry in the series in the last decade, moreso than anything, the base game moreso than Iceborne (which was by far the best part of that game). Anything interesting or compelling gameplay-wise is gone. World's awful heavy-handed story? Back and 10x worse than before. The whole game is plays itself as you listen to asinine dialogue that drags on and on as the game forces you to go places and do things you have no interest in. When you aren't lucky enough to be in a cutscene, every line of dialogue is followed by a 5 second pause that makes it feel unnerving and awkward. All the interesting and unique changes from Rise/Sunbreak (no hot/cold drinks, palamutes, weapon skills, &c.)? Gone completely. The game literally won't even let you upgrade your own armor until you're quite deep into it. All hunts are short and barely interesting and you can craft all a monster's equipment after just one or two hunts. Capcom even had the brilliant idea to remove the ITEM BOX. All of which is to say nothing of the horrible performance and constant stutter that makes even attempting to play this game a migraine-inducing hell. This easily takes the cake as my least favorite entry into the series (even acknowledging the abysmal MHST2). I pray for a decent Sunbreak save transfer tool to crop up, because all this game has managed to do is make me wish I was playing an actual good game. A beautiful game and a testament to the fidelity with which Capcom can produce a title, but utterly horrid AAA drivel to play. I will not be playing the next main-series entry. 4/10

The game is definitely fun, although you will likely have to look up guides on the internet to explain certain features and gameplay mechanics. Some skill descriptions are vague and there is no in game description (that I can find) of what certain buffs do so I had to look up external guides for those. This wasn't really a problem for me personally but I can see it being frustrating that the game doesn't provide you all the information you might need to make informed decisions. The addition of focus mode is a significant improvement IMO in terms of combat effectiveness, being able to change the direction of your attacks is huge for this game and has made it much more fun. The game has felt a bit easier than Monster Hunter World, althogh that may just be because I'm more experienced now but I have only failed 1 hunt in my time playing, and that is against what is considered the most difficult monster in game so far, but I've still been enjoying my time and am looking forward to whatever new content they add.

It makes me miss the other titles of just, here's a short cutscene, cool now post quest and have at it.

Now I have no incentive to build units until the last game because I will be forced to reset. This games forced balance is forced upon us to attract people who don't like 4X. They are trying to cast a wider net at the expense of core players. This paired with upcoming DLC to finish this unfinished game has me pretty upset. As a longtime CIV fan this game has massive, massive potential. The map is astoundingly beautiful, the new leaders are pretty solid (minus the drawings) and the new civs as well, and things like navigable rivers are so cool for strategic military moves and can make ships relevant for land warfare, However, the game in its current state tips just barely into the category of not enjoyable simply based on how the game triggers certain events and how the AI plays. The ages feature is completely immersion breaking and it's really difficult to stay engaged when the empire you've spent hundreds of turns funding and building is reset at the start of the next age. There are ways around this, for example you save your cities by spending coins in the prior age to ensure thorough building for a higher population, convert to a city, then when it comes time for the next age you're looking at 200-500 coins to turn it back to a city on Turn 1. Granted that's not cheap but if you've built an average economy it's fine-ish. Military you can avoid the reset by focusing on commanders first then units to pack into them. One of these major changes wouldn't be bad but paired with the AI forward settling and rationale behind declaring wars, it makes it nigh on impossible to 1. play anything other than a militaristic game, 2. properly grow towns if placed anywhere near an AI, 3. plan any sort of expansion on any level above Governor. The problem has been discussed at length on Reddit so won't expand here but until the March patch, hold off on the purchase.

I suppose I'll start with the positives about this game. It is fun to play. The new ages system is surprisingly well implemented compare to other games that have tried similar mechanics. The game has really high potential. Now, on to the negatives, and there are plenty of them. Let's start with the problem everyone seems to have -- the UI. It's ugly, it's got several bugs, and it's not very intuitive. The tutorial that explains it does a mediocre job and is extremely obnoxious with all of the pop-up boxes all over the place. The Civ 6 tutorial messages were much less intrusive, so that's a nasty downgrade. A LOT of people have issues with it, and I'm no different. Next up is the low number of civs and leaders. Look, I know the game is new, but this is less than both Civ 5 and Civ 6 had at startup. I also get that it will be expanded upon later, but that brings me to my final MAJOR issue with the game -- the monetization. Like far too many new games these days, the game feels like it has had important parts cut off prior to launch for the sole purpose of squeezing the fans for more money, whether that be at launch with the hefty price tag to get everything, or later with the cost of DLC. This has been a problem with most AAA games for years now and it just seems to get more egregious with every passing year. In conclusion, I cannot recommend this game to others in the state it is currently in, nor can I recommend that others pay the current price for it. I am having fun with it and will not be refunding or anything like that, but that is purely because I can see the potential after having played it. That potential needs to be realized before I can advise anyone to buy the game. It should have been whole at launch.

Like many others, I've also been a loyal Civ player for 30 years and was very excited for the new iteration. Civ VI has been my favourite, although it took some getting used to compared to the previous ones. Civ VII, though absolutely stunning from a graphics point of view, comes as a pretty big disappointment, unfortunately. I appreciate the fresh take on historical timelines, but part of the fun of playing Civ has always been that you could play the game whichever way you wanted. It allowed us to explore any combination of leader personality and player choices throughout the game. Because Civ VII severely limits these choices, it stunts what could have been a great experience. For example, not being able to cross the ocean until the Exploration Age makes sense historically, I suppose, but it also makes for a very linear, predictable and ultimately boring game. The player has no choice but to wait and then go explore at a prescribed moment. Another example is that during age transitions, players have no influence over certain changes that are invariably going to happen: cities are suddenly no longer cities, peace treaties are made without the player having a say in it, units are automatically upgraded, city recources are redistributed etc. This kind of thing makes me wonder who is in charge of the game I'm playing. It should be me, surely? Overall, it is a visually beautiful game, it is rich in detail and brings some lovely new features (such as overbuilding, new wonders and units, new leader personalities, narrative choices etc.), but to me personally, the gameplay just feels too rigid. After only 6h, I have already lost interest and will most likely return to Civ VI, which I've played for 300+h.

Sid Meier's Civilization VII can be surmised by the expression "one step forward, two steps back." While the game in this incarnation has undoubtedly improved in some superficial areas such as the graphics of the map, too many key aspects of what made prior titles in the series fun feel hollow in this iteration. I love the realistic miniature models. Great People have almost been scrapped completely, with some civs having special particular great person units as a unique civ mechanic. Compared to unique great people in 6, this sucks. The UI, while clean, is an overcorrection from VI that lacks even the most basic data one might desire to see. It lacks basic hyperlinks to re-direct you, and as an example, the civlopedia (the in-game reference encyclopedia) is frankly less functional than even Civ 3 or 4's. Civ 6 also did a great job color coding things down to the individual building so as to provide clarity as to what resource x subject was associated with. Civ 7 lacks all of this. Civ 5 had the perfect UI in my opinion, with a detailed yet less is more approach. They doubled down on the sprawling aspect of one's civilization, almost any given hex can have a resource or urban district plopped down on it. For people who disliked the district change in Civ 6, or wonders taking up a whole tile, they've only leaned in further. And no more workers. Cities just instant improve when they grow. Another fundamental problem I have with this game: Content. Or the lack thereof. The tech tree is a good place to begin, and I was shocked at how bare-bones it is in this game versus others in the series. Eurekas are strangely absent, even though the infrastructure to create them is there. What I mean is that there are Eurekas to unlock certain civs in the next age (e.g. if Augustus of Rome wants to transition to Mongolia in the Exploration Era, he needs to either improve 3 Horses or own 3 Siege units). With the whole "History is built in layers" meme they've been leaning into, I expected something like research "alchemy in the age of exploration to get a boost towards chemistry in the modern age", but even that is seemingly too much to ask for. We can count the number of techs in the "Modern Age" with the fingers on our hands: Academics, Aerodynamics, Armor, Combustion, Electricity, Flight, Industrialization, Mass Production, Military Science, Mobilization, Radio, Rocketry, Steam Engine, Urbanization, AND 'FUTURE TECH'. Im sorry but this is garbage and is clearly obsolete by like 1960 historically. What happened to particle physics and stealth tech that even the likes of civ 4 or civ 5 had? As a base-game, with day 1 dlc, this is a joke. Each era I found myself researching future tech an average/upwards of 5 times. I suspect in the future we'll be getting two new ages--prehistory and information era. Thats the only way I can rationalize the lack of options that should otherwise just be there. Religion has been neutered mechanically as well. Basically in antiquity you get a pantheon automatically and in the exploration age everyone founds a religion automatically no great prophet no faith no race/competition just arbitrary global stat boosts and a new types of units for you to start mass producing to counteract AI religious unit fodder. Same with Nukes and WMDs. No tech, you just get them now. Herp de derp. Natural Disasters seem cool until you realize theres like 4 of them and you're only ever going to see the same two on repeat for the whole game. Commanders are nice, and unit stacking in this sense is the happy medium many can get behind. Treasure fleets are a cool idea, but they overlooked basic things, such as treasure fleets being permanently stuck in lakes forever. Game is a buggy mess, with riddled with frustrating bugs/crashes, many of them ruining or corrupting savegames. Where are Scenarios? There aren't even any in this dreaded DLC roadmap, so I assume we aren't getting those anymore. And where are the basic customization options that every other game had? No true earth or earth-like maps avaialable? No changing starting resources to scarce, strategic balance, abundant, etc... Really? Sid Meier's Civilization V has 43 civilizations. Sid Meier's Civilization VI has 50 playable civilizations. Sid Meier's Civilization VII has 29 civilizations. (+2 DAY 1 DLC.) Why should we, as consumers, accept less for more? This is the highest priced Civilization game ever, and yet in terms of a sequel, this title fails every metric it would've liked to have met. Thus far, I see a lot of beloved mechanics scrapped from previous games. I find it utterly distasteful that they will likely be reselling us the same mechanics we already had in increments of $30 dlcs. Im not sold on disconnecting leaders from their civs either. Why not just choose a new leader along with a new civ per age? That makes more sense to me than civilizations like Egypt being locked to antiquity when Egypt was present in all three of the game's ages. There's just something so jarring and confusing about Rome or the Achaemenids declaring war on you and then being shouted at by Harriet Tubman of America. What was Firaxis thinking?!

There is enjoyment to be had for any strategy game fan, and the core "Civ Experience" is intact and improved upon from past iterations, but the game which surrounds this design is woefully unpolished and barely adequate for a $70 price tag. Much has been made about the atrociously unpolished UI, which really is that bad, but this same "cobbled-together" feel applies to almost every interaction-based system in the game. It just feels "off" to play and a distinct lack of feedback from the controls or menu buttons persist throughout every mouse click. I'm sure when this game has received several significant patches, that the core will shine through as a worthy installment in the series, but as of release, it feels as if Firaxis suddenly had their deadlines pushed up by several months to satisfy publisher's quarterly earnings goals. This game is unfinished and laughably rough for a product of its caliber and asking price.

In 1994 Sid Meier released a fun little game Sid Meier's colonization. Somehow with Civ 7, the makers succeeded in taking a little bit out of that game and wrongly implemented it in Civ 7. An arbitrary city cap for now reason, so you can basically hardly expand by peace. By war then? Nope, same city cap. Is a city wrongly placed on the map, deal with it, because razing a city magically gives all your adversaries military bonuses against you, for the rest of the game, and they stack! So no peaceful expansion, no warlike expansion. This turned the game in a really slow paced watered down Sim City, where you can buy/build some buildings. But only in some of your (artificially reduced number of) cities. This game was so boring, I just quit playing halfway through the second age. What I also missed was this Civ feeling of timelessness, slowly progressing through time. The 3 ages thing destroyed that. Also the huge map, compared to previous civilizations, is pretty small. As a fervent Civ player since the beginning, I was extremely disappointed by Civ 7. I do not recommend this game.

After giving the game and it's new features a chance I did have fun but until the developers fix the many issues present, this installment of Civ will never be as popular or re playable. Beyond the horrible UI, the game and civilopedia don't explain new features well... or at all. Want to look up radioactive fallout to see how to get rid of it since there aren't workers anymore? Good luck. Maybe it dissipates after a few turns? Not sure, the eras are too short to really find out and the game forcibly ends after a victory condition! Think you leveled up your leader to get some of those bonuses that are frustratingly locked behind hundreds of hours worth of gameplay? Guess again! The game doesn't accurately trigger most of the challenge criteria, how many full games do I have to play before it registers that I've completed the antiquity era even once! The settlement cap is a joke, you have to put up with the other Civs spamming cities near you until you can take them then have to decide whether to keep them against your limited cap or get permanent war support against you?! I'm not sure that feature even works because the cities take forever to raze vs how short the eras are. Choose to go over that settlement cap and start incurring unhappiness in your cities, what are the consequences? Do they rebel, do they not grow, do they reduce yields? Other than a one and done notice that your people are unhappy and that it's bad... I have no idea! Not to mention the city screen doesn't itemize so you learn how to fix happiness issues. Why can't I pick which building to overbuild, the game chooses for me? Why?! Why can't I deconstruct buildings because there's so many and you can't realistically city plan well based of adjacency bonuses over multiple eras. No workers..? This one is controversial, I get that workers were removed to cut down on micromanagement fatigue but then they also removed auto explore... so you are forced to micromanage that instead. The worker micromanagement fatigue was real by the end game BUT that's always how I felt that I excelled and won against the odds playing on high difficulties because I was able to extremely efficiently manage and optimize my Civ vs the average player or computer. This game tried to level the playing field for people who haven't played or casually play and don't deep dive into how the game works in order to be good. I read somewhere that the eras being split was meant to avoid the player or computers from getting too far ahead or It very much feels like cheap rubber band mechanics from early racing games where no matter how well you played the computers were rubber banded at 500 mph to catch back up with you... and people hated that 2-3 decades ago, why would they reintroduce such a horrible concept? The game is fun to play for short periods of time but the frustration will keep me from playing like I played the other games. It feels like a Civ imitation almost, this release significantly lowered my opinion of the developer's ability to either create a true Civilization main entry or realize that their work wasn't nearly ready for launch. I'll check back in a few months or a year to see if they've decided to release a real $140 quality product then.

Windows 10 & 11 has something called a RADAR_PRE_LEAK service which tries to detect a potential memory leak in an application and deal with it before it becomes a bigger problem. After uninstalling my video drivers and attempting other fixes, I began surfing other discussion boards and noticed a considerable number of submission mentioning Steam specifically. So I tried a simple test; I put Steam into offline mode. Low and behold; the issue went away. Back in Online mode; it came back. The issue is not with the game, it is with Steam during Online mode doing something that RADAR_PRE_LEAK doesn't like. If you experience this problem and see the Windows dialog box that "Sid Meier's Civilization VII (DX12) is not responding... try putting Steam in Offline mode.

Yes, the UI is bad. A completed game with a pre-alpha UI. Yes, they left out a couple of integral features like teams, a variety of map types, and map sizes. HOWEVER, they did an amazing job with gameplay and the changes to CIV's core mechanics. In my opinion, Civ 5 (in its finalized state) was a masterpiece for the time. It lacked several things, namely a variety of gameplay strategies to progress towards victory other than blitzing science first above all else. Civ 6 fixed that issue and introduced a variety of other, more dynamic strategies. However, Civ 6 screwed a lot of that up and made several mistakes in the implementation and depth of those systems. Civ 7 LEARNED from those mistakes and it finally feels like they've made the game they had intended all along. Your choices matter. They carry depth and have implications hundreds of turns down the line. There is an immense amount of variability and viability of strategies to come out on top, and I cannot wait to explore more of them. Yes, it has its issues. And it's sad that the state of gaming today is releasing unpolished, arguably unfinished games. But as far down as that list goes? Civ 7 is FAR from the bottom. Where I'd wait a year or two for most triple A games, or several years for titles like No Man's Sky to come around, I couldn't be more excited to see the state of the game a month from now, after the first major update releases with UI changes amongst everything else. Because the issues I have are minor in the grand scheme of things.
